title: Netscape, the maker of the web browser, can now be bought
what: Shares of Netscape Communications of Mountain View, California, can be bought from this month. The company was founded in April 1994 and makes Netscape Navigator, the program that most people use to look at pages on the World Wide Web, and sells server software to companies building their own web sites. On 18 September it announced Navigator 2.0. In August Microsoft launched Windows 95 together with the first version of its own browser, Internet Explorer. Netscape's revenue rose to $11.9 million in the second quarter; buyers are betting that the internet will grow fast and that Netscape will remain its main door.
why: The listing beat. The IPO of 9 August is told in tech (35251842); here the share enters the game at the end of September. The case for buying was growth and market leadership; the threat that would decide its fate, Microsoft's free browser, had just appeared.
source: https://web.archive.org/web/1998/http://home.netscape.com/newsref/pr/newsrelease43.html (Netscape press release of 18 September 1995 introducing Navigator 2.0, read 2026-10-14); https://web.archive.org/web/1998/http://home.netscape.com/newsref/pr/newsrelease56.html (third-quarter release of 24 October 1995, giving the second quarter's revenue, read 2026-10-14); https://archive.seattletimes.com/archive/?date=19970311&slug=2528165 (Seattle Times timeline: August 1995, Internet Explorer and Windows 95, read 2026-10-14); https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Netscape (read 2026-10-14)

title: Netscape's sales jump 75% in a quarter; Navigator 2.0 goes out for testing
what: On 10 October Netscape put test versions of Navigator 2.0 on the internet for free download, including a version that runs programs written in Sun's new Java language, and offered prizes to users who find bugs. On 24 October it reported revenue of $20.8 million for the third quarter, 75% more than the $11.9 million of the quarter before, and a net profit of $1.4 million after a loss in the spring. AT&T, @Home and Hewlett-Packard have signed agreements to use and resell its software, and it has opened offices in Paris, London and Munich.
why: Revenue nearly doubling every quarter was the story that carried the share: +41% in October 1995.
source: https://web.archive.org/web/1998/http://home.netscape.com/newsref/pr/newsrelease48.html (press release of 10 October 1995, read 2026-10-14); https://web.archive.org/web/1998/http://home.netscape.com/newsref/pr/newsrelease56.html (press release of 24 October 1995, read 2026-10-14)

title: Netscape splits its shares; its founder is now a billionaire
what: Netscape said on 14 November that it will split its shares two for one in January, only three months after going public. Its shares then rose further after Rick Sherlund, the software analyst of Goldman Sachs, said that smaller, nimbler internet companies threaten late-comers such as Microsoft; he lowered his rating of Microsoft and raised Netscape's. The 19-month-old company is now worth about $4 billion on the stock market, and the stake of its chairman and co-founder Jim Clark, who started it with $4.1 million, is worth more than $1 billion.
why: The peak of the first internet mania: +57% in November 1995. The share peaked on 5 December, just before Microsoft announced its internet strategy.
source: https://www.spokesman.com/stories/1995/nov/18/netscape-founder-hits-jackpot-jim-clarks-41/ (Spokesman-Review, 18 November 1995, read 2026-10-14); https://archive.seattletimes.com/archive/?date=19970311&slug=2528165 (Seattle Times, on the Goldman Sachs rating change of November 1995, read 2026-10-14)

title: Microsoft gives its browser away; Netscape's shares fall
what: Netscape began shipping Navigator 2.0 on 5 February, with more than a thousand small Java programs already written for it. But its shares, which peaked in early December, have fallen hard. On 7 December Bill Gates said Microsoft would embrace the internet and give its own browser, Internet Explorer, away, 'free forever', while Netscape asks companies and most users to pay for Navigator. And six months after the public offering, employees who had agreed not to sell 22.8 million shares are now free to sell them.
why: The first big blow: -38% in February 1996. Microsoft's turn to the internet (Gates's 'Pearl Harbor Day' speech) made investors doubt that Netscape could keep its lead; the end of the lock-up added sellers.
source: https://web.archive.org/web/1998/http://home.netscape.com/newsref/pr/newsrelease82.html (press release of 5 February 1996, read 2026-10-14); https://archive.seattletimes.com/archive/?date=19970311&slug=2528165 (Seattle Times on Gates's speech of 7 December 1995, read 2026-10-14); https://archive.seattletimes.com/archive/19960316/2319160/netscape-execs-sold-shares-as-stock-fell (Seattle Times, 16 March 1996, on the lock-up of 22.8 million shares and the fall since December, read 2026-10-14)

title: Netscape beats forecasts as the Nasdaq sets records
what: Netscape reported on 23 April revenue of $55 million for the first quarter, 35% more than in the last quarter of 1995, and a profit of $4.7 million, or 6 cents a share, more than Wall Street expected. It is shipping Navigator 2.0 and has unveiled SuiteSpot, a set of server programs for companies' internal networks, or 'intranets'. Its shares rose for two days in a market that loves technology: on 24 April the Nasdaq index closed at a record for the fifth day running, on the busiest day in Wall Street's history. On 29 April Netscape introduced Navigator 3.0.
why: Recovery on results and the spring 1996 technology rally: +48% in April 1996.
source: https://web.archive.org/web/1998/http://home.netscape.com/newsref/pr/newsrelease127.html (press release of 23 April 1996, read 2026-10-14); https://www.spokesman.com/stories/1996/apr/25/dow-tumbles-on-wall-streets-busiest-day/ (Spokesman-Review, 25 April 1996, read 2026-10-14); https://web.archive.org/web/1998/http://home.netscape.com/newsref/pr/newsrelease129.html (press release of 29 April 1996, read 2026-10-14)

title: Technology shares slump; Microsoft builds its browser into Windows
what: Technology shares fell sharply in July: by 25 July the Nasdaq index was 15% below its record of 5 June. Netscape reported on 18 July revenue of $75 million for the second quarter, 34% more than in the first, but its profit fell to $906,000 after $6.1 million of costs for three acquisitions. On 22 July the New York Times reported that Microsoft will build its own web browser into a new version of Windows 95 and distribute it later this summer.
why: The market's first real pullback in five years met the Microsoft threat: -37% in July 1996.
source: https://web.archive.org/web/1998/http://home.netscape.com/newsref/pr/newsrelease191.html (press release of 18 July 1996, read 2026-10-14); https://www.spokesman.com/stories/1996/jul/23/stocks-slide-again-investor-sentiment-worsens/ (Spokesman-Review, 23 July 1996, read 2026-10-14); https://www.spokesman.com/stories/1996/jul/26/nasdaq-system-takes-troubles-in-stride-blunders/ (Spokesman-Review, 26 July 1996, read 2026-10-14)

title: Navigator 3.0 is downloaded 2.5 million times in two weeks
what: The browser war is on. Microsoft released Internet Explorer 3.0 in August, and Netscape followed with Navigator 3.0 on 19 August; Netscape has also complained to the Justice Department that Microsoft breaks the law. On 4 September Netscape said that users had downloaded more than 2.5 million copies of Navigator 3.0 in its first two weeks, and that Navigator, with more than 40 million users, remains the most popular internet program in the world. Its web site now gets more than 100 million hits a day.
why: Netscape showed it could still win the race for users: +33% in September 1996, in a rising market (+5%).
source: https://web.archive.org/web/1998/http://home.netscape.com/newsref/pr/newsrelease229.html (press release of 4 September 1996, read 2026-10-14); https://web.archive.org/web/1998/http://home.netscape.com/newsref/pr/newsrelease238.html (press release of 11 September 1996, read 2026-10-14); https://archive.seattletimes.com/archive/?date=19970311&slug=2528165 (Seattle Times, on the August 1996 releases and the complaint, read 2026-10-14)

title: Analysts turn against Netscape
what: Netscape's shares have lost about half their value since the new year. On 7 January they fell almost 20% after two brokers lowered their ratings: Chrysler had chosen Lotus software over Netscape's, Apple will ship Microsoft's Internet Explorer with every Macintosh, and Microsoft gives away web server software with Windows NT. On 13 January a Merrill Lynch analyst questioned how many sales Netscape had booked in the last days of the quarter, and the shares fell another 10%. Netscape then reported 1996 sales of $346 million, up 405%, and a profit of $20.9 million.
why: The market began to price Netscape as a loser to Microsoft: -48% from the end of December 1996 to the end of February 1997 (the January close is missing).
source: https://web.archive.org/web/20250216222037/https://www.itprotoday.com/microsoft-windows/netscape-shares-fall-dramatically (WinInfo, 7 January 1997, read 2026-10-14); https://web.archive.org/web/20250216215140/https://www.itprotoday.com/microsoft-windows/netscape-stock-falls-with-analyst-report (WinInfo, 13 January 1997, read 2026-10-14); https://archive.seattletimes.com/archive/?date=19970311&slug=2528165 (Seattle Times, on the 1996 results reported in January, read 2026-10-14)

title: Netscape's first loss, layoffs, and a free browser
what: On 5 January Netscape warned that it would report a loss of $85 to $89 million for the fourth quarter, its first since going public, and its shares fell 20% to an all-time low. Browser revenue fell to $17 million from $52 million a year before, as Microsoft gives its browser away. On 22 January, with its browser share down to about 60%, Netscape said Navigator and Communicator will now be free, and that it will publish the program's source code. On 27 January it reported a quarterly loss of $88.3 million; about 300 jobs will go.
why: The low point: -34% in January 1998. The free browser and the open source code were a bold answer, but the browser business was lost.
source: https://money.cnn.com/1998/01/05/technology/netscape/ (CNNfn, 5 January 1998, read 2026-10-14); https://money.cnn.com/1998/01/22/technology/netscape/ (CNNfn, 22 January 1998, read 2026-10-14); https://money.cnn.com/1998/01/27/technology/netscape/ (CNNfn, 27 January 1998, read 2026-10-14)

title: Netscape opens its code, and investors discover Netcenter
what: On 31 March Netscape put the source code of its next browser on the internet, free for any programmer to use and improve, under the name Mozilla. In April investors started to buy its shares again, for another reason: Netcenter, the web site that opens whenever someone starts Navigator, draws a huge amount of traffic, which puts Netscape in the same business as Yahoo!, Excite and Lycos, whose shares have soared. 'It is changing from a company that had been viewed as a failed competitor to Microsoft to a company in the same business as Yahoo,' said one fund manager.
why: From software seller to web portal: +50% in April 1998. The portal value is what AOL bought seven months later.
source: https://www.fundinguniverse.com/company-histories/netscape-communications-corporation-history/ (source code posted on 31 March 1998, read 2026-10-14); https://www.deseret.com/1998/4/19/19374932/netscape-aims-to-net-business-by-turning-site-into-web-gateway/ (Deseret News, 19 April 1998, read 2026-10-14)

title: Netscape breaks even, but the market falls
what: Netscape broke even in its quarter to 31 July, better than Wall Street expected: revenue rose 10% to $150.2 million and net income was $88,000, against a loss of $45 million a year earlier. On 3 August it agreed to promote America Online's local city guides on its Netcenter site. But August was a bad month for shares: by its end the Dow Jones index had fallen more than 18% from its July record amid crises in several countries, and internet shares, which tend to overreact, fell further.
why: A market move more than a company one: -37% in August 1998 against -15% for the market.
source: https://www.theregister.com/1998/08/19/netscape_gets_back/ (The Register, 19 August 1998, read 2026-10-14); https://www.deseret.com/1998/8/4/19394690/aol-netscape-reach-accord/ (Deseret News, 4 August 1998, read 2026-10-14); https://money.cnn.com/1998/09/08/markets/marketwrap/ (CNNfn, 8 September 1998, on the fall from the July high, read 2026-10-14)

title: America Online agrees to buy Netscape
what: On 24 November America Online, the biggest online service with 14 million subscribers, agreed to buy Netscape in a deal worth $4.2 billion, paid in shares: Netscape holders will receive 0.45 America Online share for each share they own. At AOL's price that is slightly below Netscape's own share price, which had more than doubled in the past month on talk of a deal. AOL gets the Navigator browser, Netscape's business software and Netcenter, one of the ten most-visited sites. Sun Microsystems will help sell the business software. The deal is expected to close next spring.
why: The end of independent Netscape: +73% in November 1998, most of it before the announcement. From now on its price follows AOL's.

title: Netscape rises with America Online
what: Since the takeover agreement each Netscape share stands for 0.45 America Online share, so Netscape's price now follows AOL's. And AOL's shares soared in December. On 22 December Standard & Poor's said it would add America Online to its index of 500 leading shares, replacing Venator, the former Woolworth's; AOL's shares jumped more than 13% in trading after the close. Index funds must buy the shares of companies that join the index.
why: Netscape had become an AOL option: +64% in December 1998, against +83% for AOL.
source: https://money.cnn.com/1998/11/24/technology/aol/ (CNNfn, 24 November 1998, read 2026-10-14); https://money.cnn.com/1998/12/22/markets/afterbell/ (CNNfn, 22 December 1998, read 2026-10-14); https://money.cnn.com/1998/12/23/companies/aol/ (CNNfn, 23 December 1998, read 2026-10-14)

title: America Online completes its purchase of Netscape
what: America Online completed its takeover of Netscape on 17 March, after Netscape's shareholders approved it the same day. Each Netscape share was converted into 0.90 America Online share: twice the 0.45 agreed in November, because AOL split its shares two for one in February. Agreed at $4.2 billion, the deal was worth about $10 billion at the close, because AOL's own shares have soared since. On 24 March AOL announced a new structure with four groups, one of them serving Netscape's business customers together with Sun Microsystems, and said up to 1,000 jobs will go. AOL now has more than 16 million members and Netscape's Netcenter more than 13 million registered users. In this game, Netscape shares are converted into America Online shares of the same value.
why: The exit beat. Holders who bought at the September 1995 listing ended with AOL shares worth about two and a half times what they paid, after a fall of 80% along the way. For AOL the completed deal is the visible news of a +64% month; the rise itself was mostly the market's appetite for internet shares. Merged with the AOL arc's beat on the same event (one story per event).
